summary: Psalm 14 begins with a David-associated heading and a blunt portrait of people who deny God in the heart and act corruptly. Yahweh looks for understanding and finds universal failure, then the psalm turns toward the harm done to “my people” and “the poor.” It ends with a wish that Israel’s salvation would come from Zion and bring joy when Yahweh restores his people.
whyItMatters: This chapter gives a compact example of how Psalms can combine moral diagnosis, protest against injustice, confidence in God as refuge, and hope for restoration. Inside Book I, it belongs among David-associated prayers that speak from crisis rather than calm detachment.

context.author: The heading says “By David,” but Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection, and their historical origin is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving Psalms as public and private prayer.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over time; assigning one date to Psalm 14 from this chapter alone would go beyond the evidence.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a section dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and confidence; this poem itself names heaven, Zion, Israel, Jacob, the righteous, and the poor.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a heading, moral indictment, divine observation, rhetorical question, and final hope for restoration.

outline.heading: The fool’s denial and corruption
outline.note: The poem opens with the heading and describes the fool’s inner denial of God, corrupt deeds, and the absence of anyone doing good.

outline.heading: Yahweh searches humanity
outline.note: Yahweh looks from heaven for understanding and seeking, but the answer is that all have gone aside and become corrupt.

outline.heading: The workers of iniquity exposed
outline.note: A question confronts those who consume God’s people and do not call on Yahweh.

outline.heading: Fear, refuge, and the poor
outline.note: The psalm says God is with the righteous generation and that Yahweh is the poor person’s refuge, even when that person’s plan is frustrated.

outline.heading: Hope from Zion
outline.note: The psalm closes with a longing for Israel’s salvation, restoration of fortunes, and joy for Jacob and Israel.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. By David. The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt. They have done abominable deeds. There is no one who does good.
keyVerses.why: This opening sets the chapter’s main diagnosis: denial of God is portrayed with corrupt action, not merely as an abstract idea.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh looked down from heaven on the children of men, to see if there were any who understood, who sought after God.
keyVerses.why: This verse shifts the viewpoint from human speech to divine scrutiny, asking whether understanding and seeking God can be found.

keyVerses.text: You frustrate the plan of the poor, because Yahweh is his refuge.
keyVerses.why: This verse names the vulnerable party in the poem and gives the reason their case is not abandoned: Yahweh is refuge.

keyVerses.text: Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion! When Yahweh restores the fortunes of his people, then Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.
keyVerses.why: The final verse turns the indictment and protest into hope for Israel’s restoration and joy.

themes: denial of God and corrupt deeds
the poor with Yahweh as refuge

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David, but such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Inside the chapter, the speaking voice describes the fool, reports Yahweh’s looking from heaven, questions the workers of iniquity, and ends with a wish for Israel’s salvation.

questions.question: What does “fool” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “fool” is defined by the verse itself through words and actions: saying “There is no God,” being corrupt, and doing abominable deeds. The psalm is not giving a general description of intelligence; it is describing a moral and religious posture as the poem sees it.

questions.question: Is “There is no God” treated as private belief or public behavior?
questions.answer: The line says the fool has said this “in his heart,” so the statement is inwardly located. But the same verse immediately moves to conduct: “They are corrupt” and “They have done abominable deeds.” The chapter connects the inner claim with visible wrongdoing.

questions.question: Why does the psalm say no one does good?
questions.answer: Verses 1 and 3 repeat that there is no one who does good, and verse 3 intensifies it with “no, not one.” The chapter presents a sweeping diagnosis of human corruption from Yahweh’s searching viewpoint. Readers differ on how broadly to apply the statement beyond the poem’s immediate contrast between the corrupt and “my people,” but the wording inside the chapter is deliberately comprehensive.

questions.question: Who are “the workers of iniquity”?
questions.answer: The chapter identifies them by what they do: they “eat up my people as they eat bread” and “don’t call on Yahweh.” The image suggests ordinary, repeated consumption of others, but the poem does not specify one historical group or event.

questions.question: What does it mean that “God is in the generation of the righteous”?
questions.answer: The verse says the evildoers are in great fear because God is with the righteous generation. It does not explain the mechanism of that fear or narrate a specific rescue. The claim functions as a contrast to verse 1: the fool says there is no God, but the psalm says God is present with the righteous.

questions.question: Who are “the poor” in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 6 names “the poor” as someone whose plan is frustrated, but also says Yahweh is his refuge. The chapter does not provide social details, income level, or a named individual. Within the poem, the poor person belongs on the side of those harmed by the workers of iniquity rather than among those doing the devouring.

questions.question: What is Zion doing in the final verse?
questions.answer: The psalm hopes that “the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion.” many psalms are oriented toward Jerusalem and its temple, and Zion here functions as the place from which hoped-for rescue is imagined. The verse itself focuses on restoration, rejoicing, and gladness for Jacob and Israel.

questions.question: Does the final line mean everything has already been restored?
questions.answer: No. Verse 7 is phrased as longing: “Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion!” It then looks ahead to “When Yahweh restores the fortunes of his people,” followed by rejoicing and gladness. The chapter ends in hope, not in a narrated completion of that hope.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that marks the psalm with a performance or collection direction; such headings guide readers, though their exact original force can be uncertain.
The person described in verse 1 as saying in the heart, “There is no God,” and as connected with corrupt and abominable deeds.
Wrongdoing named in verse 4, where the workers of iniquity are described as consuming God’s people and not calling on Yahweh.
The place from which the psalm longs for Israel’s salvation to come in verse 7.
